document.title: SITREP 7: Pakistan/Afghanistan Reaction to U.S. Strikes (Islama 06448)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
document.note: [Confidential] The Pakistani military press office clarifies Gen. Ralston's presence in Islamabad on the night of the strikes. The Taliban received the U.S. letter with evidence against bin Laden but called it 'too general' to warrant extradition, and are 'not in favor' of talks with the U.S. after the missile strikes. Excised.

ON AUGUST 25, TALIBAN LEADER OMAR WAS SAID TO HAVE REJECTED A U.S. OFFER FOR TALKS

events.description: US missile strikes on Usama bin Ladin's terrorist network/camps in Afghanistan.
Gen Ralston stopped over at Islamabad airport 7:30–10:30 PM, met Gen Karamat, told him of ships possibly for action against terrorist camps in Afghanistan.
Omar interview saying Taliban 'not in favor' of talks with US.
Omar reported to have rejected US offer for talks; Wakil Ahmed said Taliban received a letter from the US Embassy in Islamabad.
Demonstrations in Lahore against US strikes.
Expected Jamaat-i-Islami youth wing demonstration in Islamabad, with 27-28 Aug demonstrations in various cities.
U.S. missile strikes on Usama bin Ladin's terrorist network camps in Afghanistan.
Gen Ralston stopped over at Islamabad airport and met Gen Karamat, who raised the matter with the Prime Minister.
Demonstrations in Lahore against the U.S.
ISPR released an official statement explaining Ralston's presence and denying Pakistani foreknowledge.
Expected large Jamaat-i-Islami youth wing demonstration in Islamabad, with a petition delivered to the Embassy.
Gen. Ralston made a brief stopover at Islamabad airport and met Gen. Karamat about U.S. ships off the Pakistan coast, the evening of the U.S. air strikes.
ISPR issued an official statement explaining Ralston's presence and denying Pakistani foreknowledge of the U.S. attack.
Omar interview in which he said the Taliban were 'not in favor' of talks with the U.S.
Omar was reported to have rejected a U.S. offer for talks.
BBC Pashtu Service interviewed Wakil Ahmed, who said Taliban received a U.S. letter and did not want talks because of the missile strikes.
UN security officials possibly to travel to Kabul to check on the situation.
A UN expatriate was shot and UN facilities in Herat and Jalalabad were attacked the week before.

sources_cited: ISPR official statement on Ralston stopover
key_claims: Pakistan remained basically calm after the 20 Aug 1998 US strikes, with only extremists agitating.
Pakistani military stated it had no foreknowledge of the US attack, explaining Gen Ralston's 20 Aug stopover as a response to queries about US ships.
Taliban leader Omar publicly declined talks with the US, though AIP suggested the wording was softer ('not in favor').
Taliban said a US Embassy letter's claims about bin Ladin were 'too general'.
Jamaat-i-Islami and Harakat ul Ansar were seen as potential threats to Americans, especially in NWFP.
Taliban appeared to be protecting UN sites after attacks in Herat and Jalalabad.
